earlier_scan.source_named: Lobel, Jason W. 2013. Philippine and North Bornean languages: issues in description, subgrouping, and reconstruction. PhD diss., U Hawaii (covers SW Sabah phonologies)

sources.citation: OLAC / SIL Language & Culture Archives listings for [bsy] (Internet Archive copy 2015, 2024): six 1979 SIL survey wordlists (Kilugus KP, Kerukan KP, Batandok BT, Limbawang BT, Padas Damit BT, Kukut BT), Dunn 1984, Ethnologue, Glottolog; no language description listed.
Md. Roslan bin Suhailin. 2020. Daya hidup bahasa Bisaya sebagai bahasa etnik minoriti di Sabah. PhD thesis, Universiti Putra Malaysia (front matter, ch.1, bibliography; CORE 554830794).
sources.note: Nothing (language-vitality study); bibliography points to Aminah Awang Basar 2012 'Bahasa Bisaya: mengimbau kajian lampau' (ResearchGate, unreachable).

sources.citation: Lobel, Jason William. 2013. Philippine and North Bornean languages: issues in description, subgrouping, and reconstruction. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa (hdl:10125/101972).
sources.note: No statement for Sabah Bisaya: the language appears only in pronoun tables (4.45, 11.5) and ch. 11 subgrouping/segmental reconstructions; the dissertation's only stress remarks concern Philippine languages (sec. 8.2.9; fn. p.287) and a Blust quote on schwa (p.367).

sources.citation: Zaharani Ahmad. 2007. Proses asimilasi dalam bahasa Bisaya: analisis fonologi autosegmental. Jurnal Bahasa (Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka) 7(1): 159-180. [Sabah Bisaya of Kampung Mansud, Kuala Penyu; data from Aminah Awang Basar 2004]
sources.note: Nothing: treats nasal substitution (moN- prefix) and affixal vowel harmony only; the words tekanan/stres/aksen do not occur and the phonetic transcriptions carry no stress marks.

sources.citation: Dunn, Phyllis A. 1984. The Bisaya language. In Julie K. King & John Wayne King (eds.), Languages of Sabah: a survey report, 245-250. Pacific Linguistics C-78. Canberra: ANU. doi:10.15144/PL-C78.245
sources.note: Nothing; lexicostatistics, location, and intelligibility testing only (Bisaya-Tatana mutual intelligibility 82-88%).

sources.citation: Moody, David C. 1979. Sabah Bisaya (bsy) wordlist - Kukut BT [Beaufort]. SIL Language & Culture Archives 78597; 12 pp., 367-item Sabah Word List (1978), handwritten phonetic transcription (draft).
sources.note: No prose. Sporadic IPA stress ticks in the transcription fall mostly before the penultimate syllable (p.1 maˈjaʔat 'bad', ˈpunti 'banana', maˈkalu 'big', mʌˈmanuk 'bird', möˈpöit 'bitter', ˈinan 'body', möˈdöndöm; p.6 mʌˈdaru, məˈgilö, təˈtöpis, ʔaŋˈkayöu), with occasional final (tinaˈi 'belly') or initial (ˈtɔŋgulipös 'boil') marks. Implicit evidence only.

sources.citation: Pekkanen, Inka (compiler) & David C. Moody. 1979. Sabah Bisaya (bsy) wordlist - Kerukan KP [Kuala Penyu]. SIL Language & Culture Archives 78593; 16 pp.
sources.note: No prose; p.2 transcription ticks möˈpöit, ˈbölöu, ˈinan, möˈdöndöm, ˈlöböŋ, mʌkʌˈridi - again mostly penultimate. Implicit evidence only.

sources.citation: Pekkanen, Inka (compiler) & David C. Moody. 1979. Sabah Bisaya (bsy) wordlists - Padas Damit BT (SIL archives 78596, 29 MB), Kilugus KP (78592), Batandok BT (78594), Limbawang BT (78595).
sources.note: Remaining four SIL phonetic survey wordlists; Padas Damit is Dunn's isolated test village; more stress ticks would firm up the penultimate inference (still implicit evidence only).

sources.citation: Omar, Asmah Haji. 1983. The Malay peoples of Malaysia and their languages. Kuala Lumpur: Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka. xix+682 pp. - chapter on 'Bisayah' (Borneo Bisaya of Sabah).
